lead: Electrical safety means a patient or nurse cannot get a dangerous current from a mains-powered device. Three defences stop current reaching a body: a protective earth wire, isolation, and double insulation. Four tests prove those defences: visual inspection, earth continuity, insulation resistance, and leakage current. The same checks are used before a ventilator enters an ICU, after a monitor is repaired, and during periodic testing in a hospital. This chapter shows the classes, the leakage paths, the teaching limits, and the single-fault test that matters most.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.4: current, not voltage, damages tissue, and micro-shock reaches the heart through a catheter.

blocks.text: Mains has two wires, live and neutral, and a third protective earth wire. Class I equipment connects its metal enclosure to protective earth. If a live wire touches the enclosure, current flows down the earth wire and the fuse or breaker trips. Equipotential bonding joins all metal parts that a person can touch, so no dangerous voltage difference exists between them.

Class II equipment has double insulation: basic insulation plus a second layer, or reinforced insulation, so no protective earth is needed. Class III equipment uses a safety extra-low voltage supply, usually below 25 V AC or 60 V DC, and needs no earth either.

An applied part touches the patient. Type B is body type and may be earthed or not. Type BF is body floating: the patient circuit is isolated from earth. Type CF is cardiac floating and is isolated enough for direct cardiac contact. The F means floating, so a fault current has no easy path through the patient to earth.

An isolation transformer separates the device supply from the earthed mains, so the secondary has no reference to earth. A single contact with one live conductor then cannot drive current through the body to earth. An ELCB or GFCI compares live and neutral currents; if the difference exceeds a set value, often 30 mA for household protection, it opens the circuit.

Enclosure leakage current flows from the metal case to earth through a person touching the case. Patient leakage current flows from an applied part, through the patient, to earth. They are measured separately because the patient path is far more dangerous.

I<sub>earth</sub> ≤ 5 mA in normal condition; I<sub>enclosure</sub> ≤ 100 µA in normal condition and ≤ 500 µA in single fault; I<sub>patient</sub> ≤ 100 µA for B or BF; I<sub>patient</sub> ≤ 10 µA for CF
blocks.where: I<sub>earth</sub> is protective-earth-conductor leakage; I<sub>enclosure</sub> is case-to-earth leakage; I<sub>patient</sub> is patient leakage; B, BF and CF are applied-part types. The patient limits shown are normal-condition limits; single-fault limits are higher.

blocks.text: The earth wire resistance limit is ≤ 0.1 Ω. Insulation resistance is measured at 500 V and must be ≥ 1 MΩ. Earth leakage must be ≤ 5 mA. Enclosure leakage must be ≤ 100 µA in normal condition and ≤ 500 µA in single fault. Patient leakage must be ≤ 100 µA for type B or BF and ≤ 10 µA for type CF in normal condition. Single-fault limits are higher because the device must remain safe while the fault is present, but a device that fails only in single fault is still removed.

For micro-shock, use isolated patient inputs, keep the patient circuit away from earthed metal, and during catheter procedures ask staff to work with one hand in the pocket. That stops a second hand from touching an earthed surface and completing a current path through the heart.
A safety analyser is a meter with a mains outlet, a test load and switches for normal and single-fault conditions. Start with the device off and unplugged for inspection.

items: Visual inspection: check cords, plugs, labels, fuses, cracks and liquid spills.
Earth continuity: measure from the earth pin to exposed metal; the limit is 0.1 Ω.
Insulation resistance: join live and neutral, apply 500 V DC to earth, and require at least 1 MΩ.
Leakage current: run the device and measure enclosure and patient leakage in normal condition.
Single-fault leakage: repeat with the protective earth open, then with the neutral open. The limit is higher, but a failure still means removal.
Functional test: confirm the device works, then release it.

blocks.text: The single-fault test is the one examiners ask about. Open the protective earth and measure leakage; then open the neutral. Testing only in normal condition misses the most dangerous faults. A broken earth wire or a broken neutral may leave a device looking normal while its leakage path is changed.

figure.caption: Inspect and unplug first, then measure earth continuity and insulation resistance unpowered; then power the device and measure leakage in normal and single-fault condition, and finish with the functional test.

examples.question: A technician tests a class I ventilator. Earth wire resistance reads 0.35 Ω, insulation resistance 50 MΩ, and earth leakage current 0.9 mA with the machine running. The limits are 0.1 Ω, 1 MΩ and 5 mA. Which test fails, and what action follows?
steps: Earth continuity: measured 0.35 Ω, limit 0.1 Ω. Since 0.35 > 0.1, this test fails.
Insulation resistance: measured 50 MΩ, limit 1 MΩ. Since 50 ≥ 1, this test passes.
Earth leakage: measured 0.9 mA, limit 5 mA. Since 0.9 ≤ 5, this test passes.
Only earth continuity fails, so the leakage result is not trusted until the protective earth path is repaired.
examples.answer: Only the earth continuity test fails: 0.35 Ω is above the 0.1 Ω limit, while 50 MΩ passes the 1 MΩ limit and 0.9 mA passes the 5 mA limit. Remove the ventilator, inspect and repair the power-cord earth pin, then repeat the tests.

r_ins = 50.0

traps: Testing only in normal condition: a device can pass normal leakage and fail with the earth open. The single-fault test is the real protection.
Mixing resistance units: 0.1 Ω is an earth-wire resistance, while 1 MΩ is an insulation resistance. Do not compare them as if they were the same test.
Rejecting class II equipment for missing a protective earth: class II uses double insulation and does not need an earth wire, but it must still pass insulation and enclosure leakage.

Comparing patient leakage with earth leakage: 100 µA is the patient limit for B or BF; 5 mA is the earth-conductor leakage limit; the enclosure (case) leakage limit is 100 µA in normal condition. Do not use the wrong number.
Reversing type CF and type BF limits: type CF is stricter at 10 µA, not looser than the 100 µA limit for B or BF.

quiz.q: List the six steps of the safety check in order.
quiz.a: Visual inspection, earth continuity, insulation resistance, leakage current in normal condition, leakage current in single-fault condition, functional test.

quiz.q: Why is the patient leakage limit lower for type CF than for type BF?
quiz.a: Type CF can touch the heart directly, so even a small current can cause micro-shock or fibrillation. The limit is therefore 10 µA, stricter than the 100 µA limit for type B or BF.

quiz.q: A class I device reads earth resistance 0.08 Ω, insulation resistance 20 MΩ and earth leakage 4 mA. Limits are 0.1 Ω, 1 MΩ and 5 mA. Does it pass?
quiz.a: Yes. 0.08 ≤ 0.1 Ω, 20 ≥ 1 MΩ and 4 ≤ 5 mA, so all three measured tests pass.

quiz.q: A monitor passes leakage in normal condition but fails when the protective earth is opened. What is the likely fault and the correct action?
quiz.a: The device leaks too much when its earth reference is removed, so its insulation or its mains filter capacitance is excessive. Remove it from service, have it serviced (insulation, filter, mains-to-patient isolation checked), then repeat insulation resistance and single-fault leakage tests before use.

quiz.q: What does the F in BF and CF mean?
quiz.a: Floating: the applied part is isolated from earth.

quiz.q: Why is equipotential bonding used in a treatment room?
quiz.a: It joins exposed metal parts so they stay at nearly the same voltage. Touching two of them cannot drive a current through a person.

quiz.q: Convert a patient leakage limit of 100 µA to mA.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, a safety analyser prints a pass/fail sheet that is filed with the asset number. Operating theatres sometimes use isolated power systems and line isolation monitors, so one fault does not trip the supply. Newer wireless devices remove the mains lead but bring battery, charging and radio-frequency risks. Search for electrical safety analyser and medical device periodic testing to go further.
